title: Heatwave–blocking relation change likely dominates over decrease in blocking frequency under global warming
problem: The diversity of atmospheric blocking indices hinders consistent projections of their role in future heatwaves, making it difficult to partition heatwave changes into contributions from blocking frequency, the heatwave-blocking relationship, and mean temperature increase.
method: The authors propose a method to partition future heatwave changes by first finding an optimized blocking index that best correlates with heatwaves and then using a linear regression framework to separate contributions from changes in blocking frequency, the heatwave-blocking relationship, and mean temperature in climate models.
task: The task is to partition projected changes in summer heatwave frequency under global warming into contributions from changes in blocking, the heatwave-blocking relationship, and mean temperature increase, using climate models.
innovation: This paper partitions future heatwave changes to show that the dominant driver is not the decrease in blocking frequency, but the changing relationship between heatwaves and blocking, which enhances the capacity of blocking events to generate heat, particularly over Europe.

kg_extraction_triplets.paragraph: Over Europe, with a historical heatwave frequency of 2.5%, less blocking will cause 0.6% fewer heatwaves, steepened heatwave-blocking relation will cause 1.4% more heatwaves, and the mean temperature increase will cause 60% more heatwaves.

Over Greenland, flattened heatwave-blocking relation will dominate over the insignificant decrease in blocking. The future increase in heatwave frequency is not caused by changes in blocking frequency, but by factors such as thermodynamics, that enhance the capacity of blocking to drive heatwaves.

That is, we objectively evaluate different subjective choices in blocking characteristics and find the optimized index defining the 'heatwave-driving' blocking that best correlates with summer continental heatwave frequency north of 40°N, where most Northern Hemisphere summer blocking occurs (see the section “Methods” for details).

Fig. 1 Optimized blocking index correlates well with heatwave frequency. Scatter plots of heatwave frequency versus optimized blocking index, both averaged over land points north of 40°N, in the MPI-ESM1-2-LR model. Each point represents the mean over one summer (two trailing digits of the year labelled). The ordinary least-squares linear regression line is plotted in yellow. The vertical error bars show the 1σ ranges in estimating the 10-year-mean heatwave frequency using the mean blocking frequency of the historical run (yellow, 1966–2005) and SSP585 run (blue, 2060–2099). r and R2 are shown (based only on one model and therefore slightly deviate from the multi-model mean).
